result.topic_en: Riemann discusses how sound intensities ('Schalle' of first to sixth magnitude) scale in mechanical force and amplitude. He rejects the idea that the eardrum adjusts its tension to protect against loud sounds. He also states the conditions under which the ossicles can transmit extremely small motions without losing force.

methods.what: Logarithmic intensity scale for sounds: each successive magnitude class has one tenth of the mechanical power of the previous one, so the sixth class has 10^-7 of the first.
methods.quote:
so würde die mechanische Kraft für die Schalle zweiter Größe etwa $\frac{1}{10}$, für
die dritter $\frac{1}{100}$ ...., für die sechste[?] $\frac{1}{10,000000}$ den zehn Millionten Theil

methods.what: Amplitude scales as the square root of power, so amplitudes of classes 1, 3, 5, 7 stand in ratios 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000.
methods.quote:
die Weite der Bewegungen
würde für die Schalle erster, dritter, fünfter, siebter Größe sich wie $1 : \frac{1}{10} : \frac{1}{100} : \frac{1}{1000}$
verhalten.

methods.what: Estimate of audible distance: amplitude decreases with distance from the source, scaled by a 2000-fold increase in distance.

items.english: In my view there is no reason at all to assume, for sounds at a distance of 80 ... from the source, a different ratio between the motions of the air and eardrum and the motions of the stapes footplate.

items.english: II. If the hearing organ is to transmit such small motions, as experience shows it does, then the sound conductors must fit onto one another completely exactly.

items.english: Furthermore, only a small part of the mechanical force of the motion may be lost to the purpose through other work, such as tensioning joint capsules and membranes.
